title: Ninety-nine names
hook: the Prophet ﷺ said Allah has ninety-nine names and whoever learns them enters the garden (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-asma' al-husna, the most beautiful names, given for calling. Your line was call him by his names. Which name fit a need yesterday? Day two hundred thirty-three.

Pick up a set of Muslim prayer beads, a misbaha, and count them. Very often there are ninety-nine, sometimes split into three groups of thirty-three by two small markers. Or thirty-three, meant to go around three times. Hang one in a taxi in Cairo, in a car in Karachi, on a hook in a kitchen in Dearborn. That number isn't random. It comes from a single sentence of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, recorded by both Bukhari and Muslim, with a promise attached. And the sentence has been argued over, lovingly, for more than a thousand years: what exactly the number means, and what it means to know the names. Today: ninety-nine names.
screen: `PRAYER BEADS IN A TAXI.` → `NINETY-NINE, OR THIRTY-THREE THREE TIMES.` → `ONE SENTENCE, AND A PROMISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the hadith, in paraphrase. Allah has ninety-nine names, one hundred minus one. Whoever ahsaha them will enter the Garden. And then: He is odd, witr, and He loves what is odd. Everything turns on one verb, ahsaha. At its simplest it means to count, to number off. But the scholars didn't stop at counting. Some said it means to memorize them. Others: to understand them. Others: to live by them, so that knowing the Merciful makes you merciful, and knowing the Patient makes you patient. Most said a real ahsaha holds all of these. Counting is the door. Living is the house. Then a surprise. The hadith gives the number, but not the list. The list most people learn, the one sung in schools and printed on posters, comes from a later report in Tirmidhi's collection, and many hadith scholars think it was put together by a narrator, not spoken by the Prophet. Other early lists differ by a few names. And the names in the Qur'an itself, counted up, come to more than ninety-nine. There's even a du'a, recorded by Ahmad, asking Allah by every name He has, including names He has kept hidden in His own knowledge. So most scholars understood the hadith this way: not that Allah has only ninety-nine names, but that there are ninety-nine that come with this promise. Ninety-nine doors, and more behind them. You don't need to walk through all of them this month. We'll take a first selection.
screen: `ONE HUNDRED MINUS ONE.` · `AHSAHA — COUNT, KNOW, LIVE.` · `THE NUMBER, BUT NOT THE LIST.` · `NINETY-NINE, AND MORE BEHIND THEM.` · then, large: `NINETY-NINE DOORS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and count on your fingers the names you already know. Say each one quietly and fold a finger. Ar-Rahman. Ar-Rahim. As-Salam. Al-Wadud. Al-Hayy. Al-Qayyum. Maybe al-Ghafur, the Forgiving, or al-Karim, the Generous, from a friend's name. Don't worry about how many. When you run out, rest your hands open and breathe. Each name you counted is a door you've already found. The bell holds the time.
Ninety-nine names. The number of names the Prophet said come with the promise of the Garden, for whoever counts, knows and lives by them. Today's word.
Your line: ninety-nine doors. Today, start a list: write down every name of Allah you know so far, with a few words about what each one means. Leave room. Day two hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Many Muslims learn a recited list of the ninety-nine names as children, often set to a melody, and use prayer beads of ninety-nine or thirty-three to remember Allah by His names after prayer.

fork.setup: the hadith promises the Garden to whoever ahsaha the names. what did most scholars say that asks of you?
options: count, understand and live by them
fork.reveal: counting is the door; knowing and living by the names is the house.

original.note: Arabic: counted them, encompassed them. the verb the whole hadith turns on.

trapdoor: what you thought: God has exactly ninety-nine names, and here's the list.
what it means: ninety-nine names come with a promise for whoever counts, knows and lives by them.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari 7392 and Muslim 2677 give the number only; the Tirmidhi 3507 list is often judged a narrator's addition; Ahmad 3712 speaks of names kept in the unseen.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 7392; Sahih Muslim 2677 (ninety-nine names; whoever enumerates them enters the Garden; He is witr)

notes: Hadith numbers (Bukhari 7392, also 2736; Muslim 2677; Tirmidhi 3507; Ahmad 3712) cited from memory; confirm.

Misbaha bead counts (99, or 33 with markers) vary; the script says 'very often'.
